items.title: Supporting the Lower Mississippi Delta Initiative
items.summary: The program establishes financial assistance agreements between the National Park Service (NPS) and qualified non-profit organizations to co-administer the Lower Mississippi Delta Initiative, which was authorized under Public Law 103-433.
items.description: The Lower Mississippi Delta Initiative (LMDI) was established in 1994 under Public Law 103-433 to assist with implementation of the Delta Initiatives Report, which included recommendations on natural resource protection, historic preservation, and the enhancement of educational and other opportunities for Delta residents. The initiative has actively worked to bring archeology, history, natural resources, cultural resources, heritage, and tourism projects to the region, local communities, and local organizations.
items.who: State, local, tribal and non-profit organizations.
items.uses: Funds will be granted to an eligible organization and create a sub-award program that funds local cultural, historical and natural history events that support the mission of LMDI.

items.title: Good Neighbor Authority
items.summary: The Good Neighbor Authority (GNA) is intended to expand limited federal capacity to implement and plan forest, rangeland, and watershed restoration projects by facilitating partnerships with authorized states, counties, and federally recognized Indian tribes. The GNA authority specifically allows BLM to enhance state-federal relationships and addressing cross-boundary land restoration needs to include treating…
items.description: The Good Neighbor Authority (GNA)-Restoration is intended to expand limited federal capacity to implement and plan forest, rangeland, and watershed restoration projects by facilitating partnerships with authorized states, counties, and federally recognized Indian tribes. The GNA specifically allows BLM to enhance government to government relationships and addressing cross-boundary land restoration needs to include treating insect-and disease-infested trees; reducing hazardous fuels; any other activities to restore or improve forest, rangeland, and watershed health, including fish and wildlife habitat. This type of work has reduced wildfire risk to habitat and communities; creates greater forest and watershed resilience against drought, insects, disease, and wildfire and expands much-needed work across state and federal lands. Authorized Restoration Services encompasses a broad set of restoration actions that work apply to work conducted by many BLM programs. Examples of work that could be accomplished through the GNA-Restoration include but are not limited to: fuel breaks, herbicide application, seed and seedling planting, post-fire burned area rehabilitation, salvage/sanitation…
items.who: The term “good neighbor agreement” means a cooperative agreement (Single Source or Competitive) entered into between the Secretary and a Governor or county, as applicable, to carry out authorized restoration services under this section. The term “Governor” means the Governor or any other appropriate executive official of an affected State or Indian tribe.
items.uses: Projects are primarily conducted on federal lands administered by the BLM located in the Western United States and Alaska. Projects may also be conducted on other lands to enhance state or Indian Tribe-federal relationships addressing cross-boundary land restoration needs to include activities confined to Authorized Restoration Service which are activities to treat insect and disease-infected trees, activities to reduce hazardous fuels, and any other activities to restore or improve forest, rangeland, and watershed health, including fish and wildlife habitat. The Bureau of Land Management must provide or approve silviculture prescriptions and marking guidelines to be applied to public lands in timber sale projects.
contacts: Division of Forest, Range, and Vegetation Resources (HQ-220) · Senior Weeds Specialist, · 2028490990 · wsalvers@blm.gov

items.title: Experienced Services Program
items.summary: ESP participants provide technical assistance and support to BLM in the development and execution of activities that benefit the general public and provide support to BLM employees. The program will provide opportunities to qualified individuals 55 years of age and older, who have specific technical skills and abilities not available or underrepresented at current BLM staffing levels. The ESP participants will not…
items.description: The Experienced Service Program (ESP) is a federal initiative designed to bring the valuable knowledge, skills, and experience of older Americans into the work of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). As the BLM oversees millions of acres of public lands across the United States, it relies on a workforce with deep understanding of natural resources, cultural heritage, recreation management, environmental protection, and more. Over time, many of the people who have shaped this work retire, and with them goes critical institutional knowledge. ESP helps bridge that gap. ESP serves two main groups: 1. Older Americans looking to continue contributing their skills. Under the authority provided to the Department of the Interior, the BLM partners with nonprofit organizations designated by the Secretary of Labor under Title V of the Older Americans Act. These organizations specialize in creating pathways for older adults to remain active in the workforce, share their expertise, and take part in meaningful work that benefits their communities and the nation. 2. BLM programs and offices that need experienced talent. Many BLM programs—such as energy development, cultural and natural resources,…
items.uses: This program will provide opportunities to qualified individuals 55 years of age and older who have specific technical skills and abilities not available or underrepresented at current BLM staffing levels. The ESP participants will not replace or displace current BLM employees. Recipients can use the assistance to support employment opportunities for individuals 55 years and older on projects that support the BLM mission.

items.title: Eastern Nevada Conservation, Recreation and Development
items.summary: This program advances the Department of the Interior’s role as stewards of the public lands by cultivating community-based conservation and partnerships. This program provides support and guidance for carrying out the expenditure of appropriated funds generated from the sale of public lands in Lincoln and White Pine Counties in eastern Nevada. A primary goal of this program is to carry out the inventory, evaluation,…
items.description: The program will focus funded partnerships on key activities in support of the Department of the Interior's priorities, where there is clear alignment of Bureau priorities, as well as partner goals working within Nevada’s public laws governing the expenditure of revenue generated through public lands sales. The primary purposes of this program are to carry out the protection and management of unique archeological resources, providing for recreation improvements on certain trails and wilderness areas and improving the habitat for threatened, endangered or at risk species in eastern Nevada.
items.who: State, Local, Public nonprofit institution/organization, Other public institution/organization, Federally Recognized lndian Tribal Governments, Private nonprofit institution/organization, Native American Organizations as described above.
items.uses: Projects are used to benefit lands and resources in Nevada's Lincoln and White Pine Counties. Financial assistance can be used for assisting the BLM with the inventory, evaluation, protection and management of unique archeological resources; the management, protection and/or upgrade of recreational resources and related facilities, providing related public contact/education opportunities; and the conservation of threatened, endangered or at risk species.

items.title: Energy Community Revitalization Program (ECRP)
items.popular: Orphaned Well Site Plugging and Remediation, and Restoration
items.summary: To unleash American energy and enhance public safety through grants to State and Tribal governments to plug orphaned oil and gas wells and to remediate and reclaim orphaned well sites on State, Tribal, and private lands, authorized by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and codified as 42 U.S.C. § 15907.
items.description: 42 U.S.C. § 15907 directs the Secretary of the Interior to establish programs to inventory and properly plug, remediate, and reclaim orphaned wells on State, Tribal and private lands. Tribal Grants/Assistance includes three categories of project funding: Program Development Grants, Implementation Grants, and In Lieu of Grant fund. State Grants includes three categories of project funding: Initial Grants, Formula Grants, and Performance Grants. This listing also covers a cooperative agreement to the entity legislatively authorized to perform the work proposed as outlined in 42 U.S.C. § 15907.
items.who: State, Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments, Interstate Oil and Gas Compact Commission.

items.summary: To provide funds to Indian tribal governments to support general tribal government operations, to maintain up-to-date tribal enrollment, to conduct tribal elections, and to develop appropriate tribal policies, legislation, and regulations.

items.title: Consolidated Tribal Government
items.summary: To promote Indian self determination and improve the quality of life in Tribal communities by providing greater flexibility in planning programs and meeting the needs of communities. This program allows Tribes to combine various programs and/or grants into one agreement. The simplified contracting procedures enhance program accountability by reducing paperwork and reporting requirements, and reduce Tribal…
items.description: The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA), Public Law 93-638, encourages Indian self-determination and tribal control over services. Through the Consolidated Tribal Government program, tribes can merge similar services for greater flexibility in planning and meeting community needs. This approach combines multiple programs or grants into a single agreement, streamlining contracting and reducing paperwork and administrative costs. As a result, tribes can provide more impactful services with Bureau funds, such as, Scholarships, Johnson O'Malley, Adult Education, and Job Placement and Training.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments.
items.uses: Funds from various Bureau programs, such as, Scholarships, Johnson O'Malley, Adult Education, and Job Placement and Training can be combined into a single consolidated contract.

items.title: Tribal Self-Governance
items.summary: To further the goals of Tribal Self-Governance compacting for Tribes to administer a wide rage of programs with broad administrative and programmatic flexibility. The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA) authorizes Tribes and Tribal organizations to be funded by the Federal government to provide services that the Federal government would otherwise be obligated to provide due to the trust…
items.description: The Tribal Self-Governance Program authorizes participating tribes to enter into self-governance compacts and funding agreements through which they may provide programs, services, functions, and activities the federal government would otherwise provide. Through self-governance agreements, Federal law authorizes greater flexibility for participating tribes to shape programs to meet the unique social, economic, and cultural needs of their respective citizens.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and Consortia of Indian Tribes. There are two types of entities who may participate in Tribal self-governance: (a) Indian Tribes; and (b) Consortia of Indian Tribes
items.uses: Funds may be used by the Tribe/Consortium to provide a wide range of programs, services and activities such as social services, law enforcement, tribal courts, scholarships, social services, road maintenance and construction, forestry, agriculture, real estate services, wildlife and parks, employment and training. Except where a statute contains specific limitations on the use of funds, a Tribe/Consortium may redesign or consolidate programs included in a compact funding agreement and reallocate funds for such programs in any manner which it deems to be in the best interest of the Indian community being served.

items.title: Indian Self-Determination Contract Support
items.summary: To provide funds to Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and to tribal organizations to fund some or all of the indirect costs incurred in administering Federal programs for which direct appropriations are made to the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
items.description: The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (ISDEAA), Public Law 93-638, provides that a Tribe is entitled to receive contract support costs as provided by law pursuant to 25 U.S.C. Section 5325. This applies to Indian Affairs contracts and agreements under made under Title I and Title IV of the ISDEAA. All costs associated with a program, including CSC, must be reviewed for reasonableness, allowability, and allocability based on the terms of the agreement and applicable cost principals. Further, all costs associated with a program, including CSC must be reviewed for duplication of funding for cost among cost categories, the Section 106(a)(1) amount (Secretarial Amount), Direct CSC, Indirect CSC, Pre-award CSC, and Start-up CSC.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and tribal organizations authorized by Indian Tribal Governments.
items.uses: Funds may be used in accordance with indirect cost rate proposals which have been approved by the cognizant Federal agency or for lump sum administrative cost rates negotiated with the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

items.title: Services to Indian Children, Elderly and Families
items.summary: To provide funds to Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments to administer welfare assistance programs for both American Indian adults and children; to support caseworkers and counselors; and to support tribal programs to reduce the incidence of substance abuse and alcohol abuse in Indian country.
items.description: This program funds federally recognized Tribal governments to deliver welfare, protective and social services aimed at improving quality of life for American Indian children, elderly, and families.

items.uses: Funds are provided to Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments to administer welfare assistance programs for both American Indian adults and children; to support caseworkers and counselors; and to support tribal programs to reduce the incidence of substance abuse and alcohol abuse in Indian country.

items.uses: The funds shall be used to establish endowments. Income earned on the invested funds may be used to defray expenses associated with the operation of the College, including maintenance, administration, academic and support services, and community and student service programs. No part of the net earnings of the trust fund may inure to the benefit of any private individual.

items.summary: To provide funds to perform fire protection services for Indian Tribal Governments that do not receive fire protection support from State or local government.
items.description: To provide funds to perform fire protection services for Indian Tribal Governments that do not receive fire protection support from State or local government. Funds may be used to support staff, train volunteer fire-fighters, repair existing fire-fighting equipment, and purchase additional equipment. Funds may also be used to purchase smoke detectors, fire extinguishers, fire escapes, and emergency lights for public building.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments performing fire protection services on their reservation.
items.uses: Funds may be used to support staff, train volunteer fire-fighters, repair existing fire-fighting equipment, and purchase additional equipment. Funds may also be used to purchase smoke detectors, fire extinguishers, fire escapes, and emergency lights for public building.

items.title: Indian Economic Development
items.summary: These programs assist Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments by providing the resources necessary to develop a self-sustaining economic base. The program provides opportunities for business development, the coordination and integration of programs throughout the Federal government, and the partnering of Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments with local government and the public and private business…
items.description: Assistance Listing Number (ALN) 15.032, titled Indian Economic Development, is a program run by the Bureau of Indian Affairs’ Office of Indian Economic Development (OIED). Its purpose is to help Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments build strong, self-sustaining economies. It achieves this by supporting a broad range of economic initiatives from business startups and language support systems to strategic planning and tourism. This program focuses on tribal-led economic solutions and fostering collaborative partnerships with federal, state, local, and private-sector entities. The Indian Business Incubators Program (IBIP) provides funding to established Business Incubators to serve Native entrepreneurs with start-up, early-stage, and established businesses who will provide products or services to Tribal reservation communities. These incubators offer mentorship, technical assistance, networking, and facilitate access to capital. IBIP grants support up to three years of incubation services, with possible extensions contingent upon continued appropriations and other factors. The Living Languages Grant Program (LLGP) supports efforts to revitalize Native languages by funding…
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments.
items.uses: Funds are used to administer tribal revolving loan programs and guaranty loan programs in order to develop resources to improve access to capital in tribal economies. Final approval of loan guarantees is restricted to the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Funds can also be used by Federally Recognized Indian tribal Governments to develop essential tribal ordinances and commercial business codes which provide the necessary separation and exercise of sovereign immunity between business activities and tribal regulatory activities to promote a pro-business environment.

items.title: Road Maintenance Indian Roads
items.summary: To provide limited routine and preventive maintenance on BIA transportation facilities as described below: (1) BIA road systems and related road appurtenances such as surfaces, signs, pavement striping, trail markers, guardrails, etc.; (2) Highway bridges and drainage structures; (3) Airport runways and heliport pads; (4) Boardwalks; (5) Adjacent parking areas; (6) Maintenance yards; (7) Transit facilities; (8)…
items.description: The BIA Road Maintenance program purpose is to maintain, repair and manage roads identified as “BIA owned” in the National Tribal Transportation Program Facility Inventory. Program performance is by federally recognized tribes, the BIA and other qualifying partners. It is a maintenance function not an improvement function. It serves the public who utilize BIA Transportation Infrastructure (roads, bridges, 1 ferry boat ) on tribal lands.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments with BIA transportation facilities only qualifying for this program.
items.uses: These funds are used to repair and maintain BIA transportation facilities serving Indian reservations, with particular emphasis on school bus routes and arterial highways; for snow removal, ice control, washout repair, and landslide removal; for maintenance of the 1,000 bridges on BIA roads; for operation and maintenance of a ferry across Lake Roosevelt serving the Colville Indian Reservation; and for the maintenance of public airstrips located on tribal lands. Access to these funds is restricted to tribes with qualifying BIA road miles or other facilities required to be maintained by this program.

items.title: Agriculture on Indian Lands
items.summary: To protect and restore the agricultural (cropland and rangeland) resources on trust lands and facilitate the development of renewable agricultural resources.
items.description: The grant will implement land management practices to restore degraded cropland and rangeland on trust lands while enhancing agricultural productivity and long-term viability. The program seeks to ensure the long-term viability of trust land agriculture by balancing resource conservation with productive agricultural operations.
items.who: Native American individuals, tribal governments and native organizations authorized by tribal governments, and individuals and entities authorized to make use of Indian agricultural lands and resources.
items.uses: Funds are used to support inventory, analysis, management, and improvement of Indian agricultural lands; to administer authorized use of Indian agricultural lands; and to support efforts to control noxious weeds and other invasive species on Indian lands.

items.title: Forestry on Indian Lands
items.summary: To maintain, protect, enhance, and develop Indian forest resources through the execution of forest management activities.
items.description: Implement forest management activities to maintain, protect, enhance, and develop Indian forest resources through adaptive forest management, forest health improvement, wildfire risk reduction, habitat restoration, reforestation, and related natural resource management activities in accordance with applicable federal laws and Tribal priorities.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and Native American Organizations authorized by Indian tribal governments.
items.uses: Funds are used to support activities of reforestation and commercial forest stand improvement; timber sales management; forest inventories and plans; forest program management and administration; and forest protection activities including Wild land Fire Management. Forest Inventory, Management Planning and Forest Development funds are awarded competitively.

items.title: Water Resources on Indian Lands
items.popular: Water Resources/Water Management, Planning and Pre-Development Program
items.summary: Water Management, Planning and Pre-Development for Water Resources gives Tribes the opportunity to further Indian self-determination by establishing their own priorities to manage, conserve and utilize reservation water resources on Indian Trust lands.
items.description: Water Management, Planning and Pre-Development (WMPPD) for Water Resources provides Tribes the opportunity to further Indian Self-Determination by funding necessary technical research, studies, and other information for Indian tribes to serve as informed and prudent managers of their water resources on Indian Trust lands
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and Native American Organizations authorized by Indian tribal governments.

items.title: Minerals and Mining on Indian Lands
items.summary: The objectives of the Energy and Mineral Development Program are to: (1) provide funds to Tribes to perform technical evaluations of the energy (both renewable and conventional) and mineral resource potential of Indian reservations; (2) provide Tribes with geological, geophysical and engineering reports, maps, and other data concerning their energy and mineral resources; (3) provide Tribes technical assistance on…
items.description: The Energy and Mineral Development Program (EMDP) grant provides Federally recognized Tribal entities and Tribal Energy Development Organizations with financial assistance to identify, evaluate, and assess energy and mineral resources on Indian land. The program supports projects that conduct resource inventories, assessments, feasibility studies, and other pre development analyses necessary to plan for the processing, use, and development of Tribal energy and mineral resources. Eligible resources and potential uses include, but are not limited to: biomass (woody and waste) for heat or electricity; transportation fuels; hydroelectric power; geothermal heating or electricity generation; district heating; distributed energy systems; oil, natural gas, and helium; sand and gravel; coal; precious minerals; and base minerals such as lead, copper, and zinc. Pre development studies funded through EMDP are essential for Tribal leaders to make informed decisions about resource development and to advance projects to a stage where they can pursue financing. This no cost match program reduces project risk and supports early stage project development, helping build long term economic growth in…
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribes and Individual American Indian mineral owners.
items.uses: Minerals and Mining: Funding may be used to facilitate the inventory, assessment, promotion and marketing of both renewable and nonrenewable energy and mineral resources on Indian lands. Energy and Mineral Assessments: Funds are awarded competitively to support assessment and inventory programs and/or develop baseline data, but cannot be used for development purposes.

items.title: Real Estate Programs Indian Lands
items.summary: To provide real property management, counseling, and land use planning services to individual Indian allottees and Indian tribal and Alaska Native entities who own an interest in almost 56 million acres of trust land; to provide real estate appraisal services required in processing land transactions, and to protect and enhance the Indian leasehold estate by providing individual Indian landowners and Indian tribes…
items.description: This program provides real property management, land use planning, appraisal, and lease administration services for Indian trust and restricted lands. It assists individual Indian landowners, federally recognized tribes, and Alaska Native entities in managing trust land assets, processing real estate transactions, ensuring lease compliance, protecting trust interests, and supporting the productive and sustainable use of Indian trust lands under applicable federal authorities.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments, Native American Organizations authorized by tribes, and individual American Indians.
items.uses: Real Estate Services: decision-making processes are developed through cooperative efforts with the Indian landowners for the proper utilization, development, and enhancement of Indian trust lands. Real Estate Appraisals are one element in trust land transactions and are restricted to American Indians who have an ownership interest in property held in trust by the Federal government. Lease Compliance: program resources are used to ensure that leases on trust and restricted Indian lands and their assignees comply with the terms of the leases.

items.title: Environmental Management Indian
items.summary: To determine environmental impacts of Federal projects on Indian lands; to conduct surveys of Bureau of Indian Affairs controlled Federal lands and facilities, and of Indian lands, in order to identify hazardous waste sites, evaluate the potential threat to health and the environment, and develop the necessary remedial actions; to train area, agency and tribal staff in waste management principles; and to respond to…
items.description: This is funding for Tribal environmental programs and to support individual environmental cleanup, remediation, or assessment projects on Tribal lands.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and Native American Organizations authorized by the Tribes.
items.uses: Use of these funds are two-fold. One, they facilitate the Bureau's fulfilling statutory responsibilities: they are used to prepare Environmental Assessments (EA's); advise agency superintendents on environmental quality, waste disposal and cultural resource management; assist area offices in gathering information for EA's and Environmental Impact Statements (EIS's); review proposed actions to determine compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA); and assist area offices in obtaining information for compliance with the National Historic Preservation Act and the Archeological Resources Protection Act. Two, they are used for individual tribal projects that enhance or protect the local environment.

items.title: Indian School Equalization

items.title: Indian Child and Family Education
items.summary: The Family And Child Education (FACE) program is designed to serve families with children from prenatal to age 5 in home and center-based settings. Families may receive services in one or both settings. FACE provides early childhood for all children from birth - to age five and adult education for their parents through family literacy, parental involvement, increasing school readiness, high school graduation rates…
items.description: The Family and Child Education (FACE) program is a comprehensive family literacy program that serves eligible American Indian families with children from the prenatal stage through age five. The program strengthens families by providing integrated services through Family Enrichment (home-based), Prekindergarten, and Adult Education, recognizing parents and caregivers as a child's first and most important teachers. Families may participate in one or more program components based on their needs. FACE is designed to improve school readiness, strengthen parent and family engagement in education, support healthy child development, and increase educational opportunities for both children and adults. Through culturally responsive instruction and family-centered services, the program promotes early language and literacy development, parenting education, adult education, and positive parent-child interactions that support lifelong learning. What makes FACE unique is its multigenerational approach to education. Rather than focusing solely on the child, the program supports the entire family by combining high-quality early childhood education with adult learning opportunities and parent…
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and tribal organizations authorized by Indian tribal governments on reservations with Bureau of Indian Education funded elementary schools may apply to administer the program.
items.uses: Funds must be used for early childhood education, adult education and parenting skills. Funds may not be used for administration or construction.

items.title: Bureau of Indian Affairs Facilities Operations and Maintenance
items.summary: To provide funds for basic operating services to Bureau-owned or Bureau-operated non-education facilities and to maintain these facilities in a safe operating condition for the conduct of Bureau programs.
items.description: This program provides funding to support the basic operation, maintenance, and repair of Bureau-owned and Bureau-operated non-education facilities. The funding helps ensure these facilities remain safe, functional, and capable of supporting the delivery of Bureau programs and services. Assistance is authorized under the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (Public Law 93-638), as amended (25 U.S.C. § 450).
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments who have Bureau-owned or Bureau-operated facilities on their reservation.
items.uses: Funds may be used for essential services for non-education physical plant and utility systems throughout the Bureau. The Operation and Maintenance may be used for personnel services, supplies, materials, equipment and support for planning, reporting and managing the operations and resources of the organization as well as heating, cooling, electricity, water, sewage, refuse disposal, basic telecommunications equipment, unscheduled and preventive maintenance, GSA vehicle rental, lease agreements, and custodial and protection services.

items.title: Endangered Species on Indian Lands
items.summary: To comply with the Endangered Species Act, the Northern Spotted Owl Recovery plan, and to implement the Endangered Species Recovery on Indian lands.
items.description: Provides competitive funding to Tribes to achieve compliance with Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act for the utilization, development, or management of Trust Resources, as well as for projects that benefit Federally listed threatened and endangered or tribally significant species on Trust lands.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and Native American Organizations authorized by Indian tribal governments whose reservations are in areas inhabited by these specific endangered species.
items.uses: The program monies are species specific. Appropriated funds allow those tribes in areas of endangered species to conduct activities that are necessary to comply with the Endangered Species Act.

items.title: Litigation Support for Indian Rights
items.summary: Litigation Support funds are available for tribes who are involved in litigation, negotiation or administrative proceedings to protect tribal trust resources or tribal rights (except for tribal water rights) and need funds to cover costs associated with developing evidence, for research services, or to procure the services of expert witnesses to support the tribe’s position.
items.description: Litigation Support funds are available for tribes who are involved in litigation, negotiation or administrative proceedings to protect tribal trust resources or tribal rights (except for tribal water rights) and need funds to cover costs associated with developing evidence, for research services, or to procure the services of expert witnesses to support the tribe’s position. Approved funding for this program has been set at a rate not to exceed $200.00 per hour. (Funds for water rights issues are available from the BIA Water Rights Negotiation/Litigation Program.)
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and Native American Organizations authorized by these Tribes.
items.uses: This program supports requests from tribes for expert witnesses, research, data collection, technical support, and other evidence-gathering activities required for the United States to defend the government's position in litigation cases involving Indian rights issues such as hunting, fishing and gathering rights issues; trespass; title issues, such as property line disputes; rights- of-way disputes; allotment claims; mineral entry; pollution and other activities which have harmed or could harm the health and safety of the reservation population. Funds may be used for the payment of Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA) settlements or other payments ordered by the Courts, the Department of Justice and the Department of the Interior Office of the Solicitor.

items.title: Attorney Fees Indian Rights
items.summary: Attorney Fee funds are for legal fees (not expenses) of private legal counsel to be retained by the tribes to represent litigation, negotiations, or administrative proceedings that involve the protection of tribal trust resources or tribal rights. These funds are used to provide assistance to tribes to obtain legal representation in situations where the United States cannot represent them as authorized in 25 U.S.C.…
items.description: Attorney Fee funds are for legal fees (not expenses) of private legal counsel to be retained by the tribes to represent litigation, negotiations, or administrative proceedings that involve the protection of tribal trust resources or tribal rights. These funds are used to provide assistance to tribes to obtain legal representation in situations where the United States cannot represent them as authorized in 25 U.S.C. 175. The funds are distributed in accordance with regulations governing the expenditure of appropriated funds for the fees of private attorneys representing tribes, and the eligibility requirements are found in 25 U.S.C. 89. Approved funding for this program has been set at a rate not to exceed $200.00 per hour.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments.
items.uses: These funds are used to provide assistance to tribes to obtain legal representation in situations where the United States cannot represent them as authorized in 25 U.S.C. 175. The funds are distributed in accordance with regulations governing the expenditure of appropriated funds for the fees of private attorneys representing tribes, and the eligibility requirements are found in 25 U.S.C. 89. Bureau policy determines the attorney fee hourly rates.

items.title: Navajo-Hopi Indian Settlement
items.summary: To implement those provisions of the Navajo-Hopi Settlement Act of 1974, as amended, which are assigned to the Department of the Interior; and to institute conservation practices and methods to restore the grazing potential of rangelands lying within the former Navajo/Hopi Joint Use Area.
items.description: Implements the Department of the Interior's responsibilities under the Navajo-Hopi Settlement Act by supporting settlement-related activities and restoring the grazing potential of rangelands within the former Navajo-Hopi Joint Use Area through conservation and sustainable land management practices, consistent with applicable federal laws and tribal self-determination authorities.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments of the Navajo and Hopi Tribes and Native American Organizations authorized by either Tribe.
items.uses: Use is restricted to approved projects within the Navajo/Hopi Joint Use Area. Funds will be used for restoration of rangeland within the former Navajo/Hopi Joint Use Area (JUA). This includes livestock monitoring on the JUA, issuance of grazing permits, implementation of range management plans and grazing control methods, establishment of range units and grazing capacity, and removal of trespass livestock on the Hopi Partitioned Lands; initiation of grazing control on the Navajo Partitioned Lands; and natural resources restoration on the affected lands.

items.title: Indian Post Secondary Schools
items.popular: Haskell Indian Nations University (Haskell) and Southwestern Indian Polytechnic Institute (SIPI)
items.summary: To provide postsecondary educational opportunities for American Indian Students.
items.description: The BIE’s two directly operated postsecondary institutions, Haskell Indian Nations University (Haskell) and Southwestern Indian Polytechnic Institution (SIPI) serve American Indian and Alaska Native students from federally recognized Indian Tribes throughout the country. Haskell and SIPI utilize these funds to pay for administrative, instructional, dormitory, other support staff, supplies, materials, textbooks, and food. Haskell and SIPI also use these funds to provide residential, athletic, and other student support services.
items.who: American Indians and Alaskan Natives.
items.uses: Students may attend one of two post-secondary schools operated by the Bureau of Indian Affairs with minimal charge for tuition, room and board. Married student housing is not available on campus.
contacts: Stephanie A. Conduff, Associate Deputy Director of Post-Secondary Education · (202)208-3559 · stephanie.conduff@bie.edu
Sharon Pinto, Deputy Director School Operations · 505-563-5235 · sharon.pinto@bie.edu

items.title: Indian Graduate Student Scholarships
items.summary: To provide financial aid to eligible Indian students to enable them to obtain advanced degrees.
items.description: Non-competitive grants to Native Forward and the American Indian Law Center for scholarship opportunities and pre-law summer institute.
items.who: Individual applicants must be Indian students who are members of Federally Recognized Indian Tribes, who have been admitted to a graduate program and have unmet financial need.
items.uses: Grant funds may be used to defray the costs of obtaining a graduate degree.
contacts: Sharon Pinto, Deputy Bureau Director School Operations · 505-563-5235 · sharon.pinto@bie.edu

items.title: Indian Vocational Training United Tribes Technical College
items.summary: To provide vocational training to individual American Indians through the United Tribes Technical College, located in Bismarck, North Dakota.
items.description: Non-competitive 638 CONTRACTS to TWO tribal technical colleges and universities for the basic funds to provide additional funds for an endowment account.
items.who: Application to administer the program is limited to the United Tribes Technical College. Individual American Indian applicants must be a member of a Federally Recognized Indian Tribe, be in need of financial assistance, and reside on or near an Indian reservation under the jurisdiction of the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
items.uses: Financial aid is used to assist individual Indians to obtain a marketable skill through vocational training at the United Tribes Technical College, located in Bismarck, North Dakota. Restricted to American Indian people who are determined eligible for these services.

items.title: Indian Job Placement United Sioux Tribes Development Corporation
items.summary: To provide job development, counseling, social adjustment guidance, and referrals to job training programs and other assistance programs through the United Sioux Tribes Development Corporation, located in Pierre, South Dakota.
items.description: Provides job development, career counseling, social adjustment guidance, and referrals to vocational training and supportive assistance programs through the United Sioux Tribes Development Corporation in Pierre, South Dakota. The program assists eligible Native American individuals in preparing for, obtaining, and maintaining employment while promoting economic self-sufficiency under applicable federal Indian workforce development authorities.
items.who: Application to administer the program is limited to the United Sioux Tribes Development Corporation. Individual American Indian applicants must be a member of a Federally Recognized Indian Tribe, be in need of financial assistance, and reside on or near an Indian reservation under the jurisdiction of the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
items.uses: Financial aid is used to assist individual Indians in finding permanent employment. A weekly or monthly (depending on type of services received) stipend is paid until the participant is employed. Upon receiving employment, assistance may be provided until the first full paycheck is received.
contacts: Sharon Pinto, Deputy Director School Operations · 505-563-5235 · sharon.pinto@bie.edu

items.title: Replacement and Repair of Indian Schools
items.summary: Providing safe, functional, code-compliant, economical, and energy efficient education facilities for American Indian students attending Bureau of Indian Affairs owned or funded primary and secondary schools and/or residing in Bureau owned or funded dormitories. Additional objectives include having a demonstrated or potential ability to deliver programmatic results, optimizing economic activity and the number of…
items.description: Facilities Improvement and Repair: Funds are provided for advanced planning, design and construction for facilities improvement and repair of education facilities for the direct support of primary and secondary schools and/or dormitories. Replacement School Construction: Funds are provided for advanced planning, design and constructions of major expansions or major replacements of funded education facilities for the direct support of primary and secondary schools and/or dormitories.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and Tribal Organizations, including School Boards, who have a prioritized Replacement School Construction or Facilities Improvement and Repair, for which funds have been specifically approved through the appropriation process.
items.uses: Replacement School Construction: Funds are provided for advance planning, design, and construction of major expansions or major replacements of Bureau of Indian Affairs owned or funded education facilities for the direct support of primary and secondary schools and/or dormitories. An education facility may include an entire school facility or building, or a component(s) of a school facility or building, such as, classrooms, multi-purpose rooms or gymnasiums, or cafeteria/kitchens; and may include other improvements to real property such as, water storage tanks, water and sewer distribution lines, parking lots, and other site improvements. School facilities are replaced only in those instances where rehabilitation and upgrading are not feasible because of eligible American Indian student capacity needs, functional changes or costs. Facilities Improvement and Repair: Funds are provided…
contacts: David Whoolers, Supervisor, Branch of Facilities Management · 505-362-8974 · david.woolers@bie.edu

items.title: Safety of Dams on Indian Lands
items.summary: To improve the structural integrity of dams on Indian lands, including operations and maintenance of these dams.
items.description: The Bureau of Indian Affairs’ (BIA) Safety of Dams (SOD) Program was established under the Indian Dams Safety Act (IDSA) of 1994, P.L. No. 103-302, 25 U.S.C. § 3801 et seq. SOD’s principal authorities include, but are not limited to, 25 U.S.C. §§ 3801 – 3805, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Federal Guidelines for Dam Safety. The mission of SOD is to reduce the potential loss of human life and property damage caused by dam failure by making dams under the administration of the BIA as safe as practically possible. SOD endeavors to ensure that its dams are maintained in satisfactory condition on a long-term basis and to promote awareness and access to the beneficial uses achieved through public investments in SOD dam infrastructure. When applicable, SOD program funds are awarded through Federal Acquisitions Regulation contracts.
items.who: Federally Recognized Indian Tribal Governments and Native American Organizations authorized by Indian tribal governments to be benefited by the award.
items.uses: Funds allow for the inspection, operation and maintenance, early warning systems, and emergency action plans of high and significant hazard dams under the responsibility of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, and for safety of dam rehabilitation construction necessary to correct identified deficiencies on the most unsafe dams. Financial awards are specific to a given site and awards are restricted to Indian tribes or tribal organizations affected by the projects.
contacts: William Shuter, Acting Division of Water and Power Chief · 575-770-8457 · William.Shuter@bia.gov

items.title: Tribal Great Lakes Restoration Initiative
items.summary: The BIA Tribal GLRI Program offers financial support to Great Lakes Tribes, enabling them to carry out a wide range of projects aimed at protecting, enhancing, and restoring the Great Lakes ecosystem. Through this program, Tribes receive resources to help address environmental challenges affecting their communities and the natural surroundings they rely on. Priority actions under the program include identifying…
items.description: The Tribal Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) has helped strengthen the ability of Tribal Nations to take part in shared decision making about Great Lakes resources. This support ensures that Tribes have the tools, funding, and opportunities needed to participate meaningfully when governments work together to manage and protect the basin. GLRI investments have also expanded community education and awareness, helping Tribal Nations share cultural teachings, subsistence practices, and traditional knowledge with Tribal youth and neighboring communities. The program provides dedicated funding for Tribal Nations to carry out their own priorities for restoring and protecting the Great Lakes. Tribes can implement projects that safeguard important species, strengthen Tribal lifeways, and uphold treaty reserved rights. The program supports a true government to government relationship, giving Tribes the flexibility to design and lead projects that best serve their communities and their lands. The program supports both Tribal capacity and on the ground restoration work. It funds the staff, training, and resources needed for long-term Tribal environmental programs, while also…
items.who: Federally-recognized Indian Tribes and Native American Organizations authorized by Indian tribal governments
items.uses: This funding opportunity under the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative will be used to address tribal priorities for the Great Lakes Basin ecosystem and fall into five major focus areas: • Toxic substances and Areas of Concern, including pollution prevention and cleanup of polluted areas in the Great Lakes • Invasive species, including efforts to institute “zero tolerance policy” towards new invasions • Nonpoint source pollution impacts on nearshore health, including a targeted geographic focus on high priority watersheds and reducing polluted runoff from urban and agricultural sources • Habitat and fish and wildlife species protection, restoration, and enhancement, including removing barriers to fish passage and targeted protection and restoration of native and endangered species and their habitats in the Great Lakes • Foundations for future restoration actions, incorporating climate…

items.title: Strengthening Tribal Nations
items.summary: To provide funding to advance nation-to-nation relationships, support Indian families and protect Indian country, support sustainable stewardship of trust resources, and advance Indian education.
items.description: Provides financial assistance to federally recognized Tribes and Tribal organizations to support Tribal self-determination, strengthen government-to-government relationships, protect Indian families and Indian Country,promote sound management of trust resources, and advance education for American Indian and Alaska Native communities, consistent with applicable federal authorities.
items.uses: Funds may be used to coordinate Tribal-Federal advisory committee meetings concerning BIA budget formulation and implementation of PL 93-638; develop communication strategies and tools, including websites to share updated information and resources; provide trainings; and conduct historical budget research and trend analysis.

items.title: HŌʻIHI Grant Program
items.popular: Heritage Opportunities in Hawaiʻi (HŌʻIHI) Grant Program
items.summary: The Office of Native Hawaiian Relations’ (ONHR) Heritage (Tourism) Opportunities in Hawaiʻi (HŌʻIHI) Grant Program serves to implement the provisions of the Native American Tourism and Improving Visitor Experience Act (NATIVE Act), 25 U.S.C. 4351 et seq. The purpose of the NATIVE Act is to establish a more inclusive national travel and tourism strategy that has the potential to deliver significant benefits for…
items.description: The HŌʻIHI Grant Program is an innovative initiative aimed at leveraging Hawaiian traditional knowledge to support economic development within the NHC, promote economic growth in Hawaiʻi, and provide Native Hawaiian organizations (NHO) with the needed resources to transform tourism into a regenerative and collaborative industry. Through the HOIHI Grant Program, NHOs lead the way in creating authentic experiences that reflect their values, knowledge, and practices, ensuring that cultural traditions are honored and transmitted in ways that are meaningful to the Community itself. By restoring decision-making regarding hoʻokipa (hospitality) practices to the Native Hawaiian Community, this program fosters a future where tourism serves as a platform for integrity and self-determination, rather than simply commodification. The HŌʻIHI Grant Program additionally seeks to increase economic development within the NHC by expanding opportunities for entrepreneurship among members, increasing innovation potential on the usage and incorporation of traditional knowledge, and ultimately increasing growth of new businesses within the Community. This, in turn, broadens the ability of Native…
items.who: Nonprofits that do not have a 501(c)(3) status with the IRS, other than institutions of higher education. Native American tribal organizations (other than Federally recognized tribal governments). Nonprofits having a 501(c)(3) status with the IRS, other than institutions of higher education. Additionally, applicants must meet the definition of and criteria for a “Native Hawaiian Organization” as defined in the NATIVE Act, 130 STAT. 847, Section 3(3), codified at 25 U.S.C. §4352(3). Criteria include: A nonprofit organization; that serves the interests of Native Hawaiians; in which Native Hawaiians serve in substantive and policymaking positions; and that is recognized for having expertise in…
items.uses: Assistance will support efforts of Native Hawaiian organizations to do the following: share about the Native Hawaiian Community as the indigenous people of Hawai‘i; use arts and humanities to help revitalize, promote economic development, increase livability; share with and engage guests in growing awareness and the perpetuation of Hawaiian culture; other section purposes.

This new federal assistance program is designed to bring wildlife agencies to…

items.title: Experienced Services Program
items.summary: The ESP program provides funding that allows agencies to enter into agreements with non-profit organizations to provide opportunities to qualified individuals 55 years of age and older who have specific technical skills and abilities not available or underrepresented at current staffing levels. Qualified individuals who are part of the ESP will support Reclamation in managing, developing, and protecting water and…
items.description: The Experienced Services Program is designed to support and augment the capacity of Reclamation to meet its' mission goals and objectives in areas where it lacks sufficient expertise, technical skills and/or capacity. Through the engagement of highly qualified workers in a temporary capacity, Reclamation can in a cost effective and efficient manner meet its strategic and mission goals in managing, developing, and protecting water and related resources and provide necessary administrative support. This program will allow Reclamation to quickly add temporary workers to support to our Federal workforce. This program will in no way displace current employees or substitute future Federal workers.
items.who: Private nonprofit organizations designated by the Secretary of Labor under Title V of the Older Americans Act of 1965 to utilize the talents of older Americans in programs authorized by other provisions of law administered by the Secretary and consistent with such provisions of law.

The ESP participants will not replace or displace current Reclamation employees. Recipients can use the assistance to support employment opportunities for individuals 55 years and older on projects that support Reclamation’s mission. Documentation demonstrating the organization’s proof of establishment under the Secretary of Labor Title V of the Older American Act of 1965.

items.title: Native Hawaiian and Alaska Native Culture and Arts Development
items.summary: The Native Hawaiian and Alaska Native culture and arts development program promotes the scholarly study of, and instruction in, Native Hawaiian or Alaska Native arts and culture; establishes programs which culminate in the awarding of degrees in the various fields of Native Hawaiian or Alaska Native art and culture; and establishes centers and programs with respect to Native Hawaiian or Alaska Native art and culture.
items.description: The Secretary of the Interior is authorized to provide grants to private, nonprofit organizations or institutions that primarily serve and represent Native Hawaiians or Alaska Natives. To be eligible, these entities must be recognized by the Governor of Hawaii or Alaska for this purpose. The grants aim to support programs that preserve, revitalize, and develop Native Hawaiian and Alaska Native culture and arts, encompassing traditional and contemporary expressions in areas such as language, history, visual and performing arts, and crafts.
items.who: Any private, nonprofit organization or institution which primarily serves and represents Native Hawaiians or Alaska Natives, and has been recognized by the Governor of the State of Hawaii or the Governor of the State of Alaska, as appropriate, for the purpose of making such organization or institution eligible to receive such grants.
items.uses: Any organization or institution which is the recipient of a grant shall establish a governing board to manage and control the program with respect to which such grant is made. (2) For any grants made with respect to Native Hawaiian art and culture, the members of the governing board which is required to be established under paragraph (1) shall- (A) be Native Hawaiians or individuals widely recognized in the field of Native Hawaiian art and culture, (B) include a representative of the Office of Hawaiian Affairs of the State of Hawaii, (C) include the president of the University of Hawaii, (D) include the president of the Bishop Museum, and (E) serve for a fixed term of office. (3) For any grants made with respect to Alaska Native art and culture, the members of the governing board which is required to be established under paragraph (1) shall- (A) include Alaska Natives and individuals…

items.title: Small Surface Water and Groundwater Storage Projects
items.summary: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, Public Law 117-58, established the Small Water Storage and Groundwater Grant Program to enhance water storage opportunities. It provides up to the lesser of 25 percent, or $30 million, for the cost of planning, design, and construction of small water storage projects that, when implemented, will increase water supply reliability, improve operational flexibility, and…
items.description: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, Public Law 117-58, established the Small Water Storage and Groundwater Grant Program to enhance water storage opportunities. It provides up to the lesser of 25 percent, or $30 million, for the cost of planning, design, and construction of small water storage projects that, when implemented, will increase water supply reliability, improve operational flexibility, and enhance resiliency of water and related infrastructure throughout the 17 western states, Alaska, and Hawaii.
items.who: Eligible recipients of the Small Storage Program funding are identified under the 1902 Act and include State, regional, or local authorities; Indian tribes or tribal organizations; or other entities such as a water conservation or conservancy district, wastewater district, rural water district, located in the 17 western United States (Reclamation State) as identified in the Reclamation Act of June 17, 1902, as amended or Alaska or Hawaii.
items.uses: Reclamation’s Small Storage Program provides cost-shared funding on a competitive basis for the planning, design, and construction of small surface water and groundwater storage projects.

items.description: In 2016, the Blackfeet Water Rights Settlement passed (PL 114-322) and the Blackfeet Tribe along with Reclamation and BIA have obligations to fulfill.

items.title: Musselshell-Judith Rural Water System
items.summary: The purpose of this act is to ensure a safe and adequate municipal, rural, and industrial water supply for the citizens of Judith Basin, Wheatland, Golden Valley, Musselshell, and portions of Yellowstone and Fergus counties in the state of Montana.
items.description: The purpose of this act is to provide federal funds to Central Montana Regional Water Authority (Authority) for the planning, design, and construction of the Musselshell-Judith Rural Water System into ensure a safe and adequate municipal, rural, and industrial water supply for the citizens of Judith Basin, Wheatland, Golden Valley, Musselshell, and portions of Yellowstone and Fergus counties in the state of Montana.
items.who: The Central Montana Regional Water Authority
items.uses: Funding to be awarded to Central Montana Regional Water Authority for the planning, design, and construction of the Musselshell-Judith Rural Water System.

items.title: Rehabilitation, Reconstruction, or Replacement of Carey Act Dams
items.summary: Section 40904(b) of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, also known as the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, authorized the Secretary of the Interior to fund the rehabilitation, reconstruction, or replacement of a dam in which construction began on or after January 1, 1905, developed pursuant to the Carey Act (43 U.S.C. 641). To be eligible for funding, the Governor of the State in which the dam is located must…
items.description: The Carey Act Dam funding is set aside for reconstruction of a dam developed under the authority of the Cary Act after 1905. The Governor of the state in which the dam is located must request the funding and determine that the dam meets the applicable criteria described in the law.
items.who: A Governor or state agency under the authority of a Governor in which the Carey Act Dam is located, pursuant to section 40904(b)(3) of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law.
items.uses: Assistance may be used on a dam developed pursuant to the Carey Act for which the estimated rehabilitation, reconstruction, or replacement, engineering, and permitting costs would exceed $50,000.
contacts: Jerome Jackson · Bureau of Reclamation · 3034452712 · jljackson@usbr.gov

items.title: Snow Water Supply Forecasting
items.summary: To fund activities to improve the skill of water supply forecasts via enhancing snow monitoring through the deployment of emerging technologies to complement existing monitoring techniques and networks.
items.description: The Snow Water Supply Forecasting listing provides assistance to improve water supply forecasting in snow‑driven river systems. Its goal is to enhance decision‑making by delivering more accurate, timely predictions of spring runoff. By advancing current monitoring methods, especially through emerging technologies, this program equips water managers with critical data, helping communities prepare for droughts, manage reservoir operations, and optimize water use. The listing serves a wide range of partners, including tribal nations, state and local governments, federal agencies, universities, irrigation and water districts, nonprofits, and private companies. By prioritizing operational relevance and measurable outcomes, the listing fosters partnerships that bridge research, technology, and real-world water management.
items.who: In accordance with P.L. 116-260, Section 1111(e), paragraph (4), Program partners with whom the Secretary enters into cooperative agreements pursuant to paragraph (5) may include water districts, irrigation districts, water associations, universities, State agencies, other Federal agencies, private sector entities, non-governmental organizations, and other entities, as determined by the Secretary.
items.uses: Snow monitoring, water supply forecasting, technology development. Funding will be awarded on a competitive basis.
