items.title: Keweenaw National Historical Park (NHP) Preservation Grants
items.summary: The Keweenaw National Historical Park (NHP) Preservation Grant program is intended to provide annual base funding to the Keweenaw NHP Advisory Commission to assist in the fulfillment of their legislated duties: to carry out historical, educational, or cultural programs which enhance understanding and preservation of the historic and cultural resources in the park and surrounding area on Michigan’s Keweenaw…
items.description: The Keweenaw National Historical Park (NHP) Preservation Grant program supports projects that preserve, interpret, and share the story of copper on Michigan’s Keweenaw Peninsula. The program provides annual funding to the Keweenaw NHP Advisory Commission and selected local partners to protect historic places, strengthen heritage programs, and improve public access to cultural resources in and around the park.
items.uses: Annual funding is to be used by the Keweenaw NHP Advisory Commission in the fulfillment of legislated duties. Annual funding is used by the Village of Calumet to cover expenses related to the administration of its historic district ordinance. Additional funding for preservation or interpretation projects may be available through special program opportunities to owners or operators of non-Federal properties containing nationally significant historic or cultural resources that are related to the story of copper on the Keweenaw Peninsula.

items.title: Alaska Coastal Marine Institute
items.summary: The purpose of the Alaska Coastal Marine Institute (CMI) program is to use highly qualified scientific expertise at local levels to collect and disseminate environmental information needed for OCS oil and gas and marine minerals decisions; address local and regional OCS-related environmental and resource issues of mutual interest; and strengthen the BOEM-State partnership in addressing OCS oil and gas and marine…
items.description: The Environmental Studies Program allocates funding for cooperative research through the AK CMI program, subject to the availability of funds. The University of Alaska (AK) invites proposals that are reviewed by a Technical Steering Committee including the University, State of Alaska, and BOEM to fund individual awards. Applications must be for scientific research projects, which are within the BOEM's area of responsibility. The majority of funds are used to support research that will enhance understanding of long-term effects of oil and gas, marine minerals, and renewable energy projects. Funds can also be used for attendance at national conferences for the dissemination of project results. Funds are not normally used for capitalization.
items.uses: The Environmental Studies Program allocates up to $1,000,000 per year for cooperative research through the AK CMI program, subject to the availability of funds. Funds can also be used for attendance at national conferences for the dissemination of project results. Funds are not normally used for capitalization.

OCSLA Section 1345 authorizes the use of cooperative agreements with affected States to meet the requirements of…
items.description: The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) Environmental Studies Program provides financial assistance to conduct scientific research that supports environmentally responsible management of offshore energy and marine mineral resources on the U.S. Outer Continental Shelf. Research improves understanding of marine, coastal, and human environments to inform environmental analyses, leasing decisions, permitting, mitigation measures, and resource management.
items.who: State agencies, public universities, and non-profits in affected states may apply. More than one institution may collaborate in the preparation of an application for assistance. Scientists from other institutions may participate in collaboration with a principal investigator from a State agency or public university.
items.uses: Applications must be for scientific research projects which are within the BOEM' area of responsibility. items.title: Marine Minerals Activities
items.summary: BOEM provides financial assistance to qualified partners to identify and evaluate OCS sediment for potential use in coastal restoration and beach nourishment projects or programs and to foster capacity building and working relationships with coastal States to address coastal erosion, coastal resilience, and regional sediment management. BOEM funds activities such as conducting state-based needs assessments;…
items.description: BOEM investments in resource evaluation and environmental research facilitate the exploration, leasing, and development of marine mineral resources found on the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS). Resource evaluation research is integrated into the National Offshore Sand Inventory and National Offshore Critical Minerals Inventory, which organize and share information about mineral occurrence and deposits on the OCS. Environmental research is critical to support decisions related to the exploration, leasing, and use/development of marine minerals. OCS sediment is often used in coastal restoration and beach nourishment projects or coastal resilience programs. Cooperative agreements with states and universities advance capacity building and working relationships with coastal States to address coastal erosion, coastal resilience, and regional sediment management. Example investments include supply and demand assessments; geophysical and geological data acquisition in specific areas on the OCS; analysis and interpretation of existing or new geophysical and geological data to delineate sediment resources or benthic habitat; development of regional stratigraphic interpretations or models;…
items.who: State agencies, public universities, and non-profits in affected states may apply. More than one institution may collaborate in the preparation of an application for assistance. BOEM welcomes proposals from qualified partners to address resource demand, resource identification, regional sediment management, and other information needs related to OCS marine minerals.

items.title: Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management State and Tribal Coordination
items.summary: To ensure that all oil, gas, and solid minerals originated on the public lands and on the Outer Continental Shelf are properly accounted for under the direction of the Secretary of the Interior, and for other purposes.
items.description: The Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management State and Tribal Coordination Program helps states and federally recognized Tribal governments carry out important oversight responsibilities for federal energy development within their jurisdictions. Through cooperative agreements, the program provides funding and support so state and Tribal partners can independently perform audits, investigations, and compliance reviews on federal oil, gas, and solid minerals leases.
items.who: State and Tribal Governments as specified in Title II of the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982, as amended.
items.uses: All projects are restricted to State and Federally recognized Tribal Governments with cooperative audit agreements executed in compliance with the Authorization above. No discretionary funds are available under this program.

items.title: State Select
items.summary: The goal of the State Select disbursement is to return a portion of federal mineral leasing revenue to states so they can plan for mineral development impacts, maintain and build public facilities, provide essential public services, and prioritize support for communities most affected by mineral extraction on federal lands. These goals ensure that states have resources to manage infrastructure, public service needs,…
items.description: State Select is a federal revenue sharing program that ensures states receive a portion of mineral leasing revenue generated from specific federally managed public domain lands. When companies produce minerals such as oil or gas from these selected tracts, the Office of Natural Resources Revenue (ONRR) collects payments and disburses funds to the state so it can support essential public services. These payments help states plan for development impacts, maintain and improve public facilities, and strengthen services for communities most affected by mineral activity. What makes State Select unique is that payments occur automatically, without applications, competitions, or grants. The federal government calculates each state’s share from actual mineral receipts and transfers those funds directly, offering transparency, stability, and a strong connection between federal mineral development and local community benefit.
items.who: There is no application process. State Select funds are available only to U.S. State governments. This program is a statutory revenue‑sharing mechanism tied to select public‑domain lands and the funds are disbursed automatically when mineral leasing revenue is generated on lands selected by the State under federal law.
items.uses: No specific restrictions on use.

items.description: The purpose of the OCS 8(g) provision is to resolve boundary disputes and ensure fair revenue sharing between the federal government and the coastal states for oil and gas resources extracted from the 8(g) zone. It is unique because: *it lies between state and federal offshore boundaries and *it is a shared revenue zone, where 27% of revenues from oil and gas leases are disbursed to adjacent coastal states.

Enhancing ports, roads, and public facilities in coastal areas. - Supporting community resilience to climate change and sea-level rise. - Recreation and Public Access 5. Development of parks, trails, and public waterfronts. - Enhancing access to natural and cultural resources. - Land and Water Conservation 6. A portion of OCS revenues also supports the Land and Water Conservation Fund…

items.title: Alaska Settlement Agreement
items.summary: ONRR shares 100 percent with the State of Alaska to be paid monthly subject to late disbursement interest for contracts, leases, permits, rights-of-way, or easements under Section 6(h) of the Alaska Statehood Act.
items.description: This listing serves the State of Alaska, ensuring it receives the funds owed from qualified mineral or land use agreements. What makes this program unique is its direct, formula based revenue sharing, which does not require applications, proposals, or competitive awards. Instead, payments are determined by law and are intended to support Alaska through predictable and transparent federal to state transfers connected to natural resource activity.
items.who: There is no application process. Only the State of Alaska may receive the Alaska Settlement Agreement funds. These funds are automatically disbursed to Alaska based on revenue collected from qualifying federal land use agreements.
items.uses: No specific restrictions on use.

items.title: California Refuge Account
items.summary: ONRR shares 40.87 percent of Oil and Gas Rents, Royalties, and Bonus Bids with the State of California.
items.description: The California Refuge Account under section 8(g) automatically directs 40.87% of oil and gas rents, royalties, and bonus bids from offshore production in the federal waters near California’s coast to the state, supporting public projects and wildlife refuges. It’s unique because the funding is distributed by law through a fixed formula—no application is needed, ensuring a predictable and dedicated revenue stream for state use
items.who: There is no application process. ONRR automatically pays the State of California when qualifying 8(g) offshore revenues occur.

items.title: Flood Control Act Lands

items.description: Flood Control Act lands are areas managed to reduce flood risk and protect surrounding communities while supporting safe water operations. They are unique because they also provide public benefits like open space, recreation, and habitat, all carefully balanced with their primary safety mission.
items.who: Revenue from acquired Flood Control land leasing generates automatic payment distributions.
items.uses: To be used as the State legislature may prescribe for the benefit of public schools and public roads of the county or counties in which such property is situated, or for defraying any of the expenses of county government in such county or counties, including public obligations of levee and drainage districts for flood control and drainage improvements.

items.title: Geothermal Resources
items.summary: The Geothermal program’s goal is to ensure that local governments directly benefit from the revenue generated by geothermal leases—such as bonuses, rents, and royalties—so they can address community needs related to natural resource development. Accordingly, the U.S. Federal Government shares 50 percent of mineral leasing revenue with the State, and 25 percent with the county.
items.description: Geothermal revenue supports counties where federal geothermal energy leasing and development occur. development. Funding helps counties plan for and manage the effects of geothermal activity, invest in essential public facilities, and support services that serve residents in geothermal regions. This program is unique because it distributes geothermal revenue directly to counties, offering a reliable source of support tied to real time energy production on federal lands. The program helps communities strengthen their infrastructure, resource management capacity, and public services, ensuring that geothermal development contributes to long term local stability and growth.
items.who: There is no application process. Only States and Counties may receive Geothermal funds. These funds are automatically disbursed to the counties based on revenue collected from qualifying federal land use agreements. items.uses: To be used as the legislature directs giving priority to those subdivisions of the State that are socially or economically impacted by the development of minerals leased, for (1) planning, (2) construction and maintenance of public facilities, (3) provision of public service.

items.title: GoMESA
items.popular: GULF OF MEXICO ENERGY SECURITY ACT OF 2006 (GOMESA)
items.summary: ONRR shares 37.5 percent of selected revenue with Gulf producing states and political subdivisions; payable annually during the year after receipt in accordance with 30 CFR Section 519.418.
items.description: The Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act, commonly known as GOMESA, is a federal law that directs a portion of offshore oil and gas revenues to coastal states and conservation programs. Its purpose is simple: to support the communities and environments most closely connected to energy production in the Gulf of America. GOMESA primarily benefits: • Gulf Coast states and their coastal communities, which receive a share of revenue to support infrastructure, coastal restoration, hurricane protection, and other local priorities. • The Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF), which receives a dedicated portion of GOMESA revenue that remains available until it is fully used. This ensures long term support for parks, public lands, and recreation projects nationwide. Several features distinguish GOMESA from other federal funding programs: • Direct, formula based revenue sharing: GOMESA ensures that states closest to offshore energy development directly receive a portion of the revenues generated. • Long term availability of certain funds: By statute, LWCF’s GOMESA funds do not expire and remain available until spent, offering program stability and planning flexibility. • Support for both…
items.uses: To be used in accordance with all applicable Federal and State laws, only for 1 or more of the following purposes: A) Projects and activities for the purposes of coastal protection, including conservation, coastal restoration, hurricane protection, and infrastructure directly affected by coastal wetland losses; B) mitigation of damage to fish, wildlife or natural resources; C) implementation of a federally-approved marine, coastal or comprehensive conservation management plan; D) Mitigation of the impact of Outer Continental Shelf activities through the funding of onshore infrastructure projects; E) Planning assistance and the administrative costs of complying with this section.

items.title: Minerals Leasing Act
items.summary: The Federal Government shares 50 percent (90 percent for Alaska) of mineral leasing revenue with States. Since 2008 payments were subjected to a two percent reduction, as required by Public Law 111-322.
items.description: The Mineral Leasing Act (MLA) enables federal government to share revenue from oil, gas, and mineral development on public lands with the states where those lands and minerals are located. These monies serve state governments, which automatically receive their share of royalties, rentals, bonuses, and other payments generated from federal mineral leases within their borders. No application is required; payments occur as revenues are collected, ensuring predictable, formula‑based support to states. What makes the MLA unique is the MLA provides states with consistent, legally mandated funding tied directly to natural resource production. These funds help states invest in planning, public facilities, and essential public services, particularly in areas most affected by mineral development, making the MLA a key mechanism for strengthening local economies and managing the impacts of energy extraction.
items.who: Only U.S. state governments can receive MLA assistance. Specific terms to help public users find the listing: • State governments • Mineral leasing revenue sharing • Federal Mineral Royalties • Public land mineral development • ONRR mineral revenue distributions
items.uses: To be used by States as the legislature directs giving priority to those subdivisions of the State that are socially or economically impacted by the development of minerals leased, for (1) planning, (2) construction and maintenance of public facilities, and (3) provision of public service.

items.title: National Forest Acquired Lands
items.summary: ONRR shares 25 percent of minerals leasing revenue with the State in which such National Forest is situated. Revenue is paid monthly.
items.description: The National Forest Acquired Lands program helps ensure that communities located near federally managed National Forest lands benefit directly from the mineral revenues generated on those lands. When companies produce minerals—such as oil, gas, or other leasable resources—from acquired National Forest tracts, the Office of Natural Resources Revenue (ONRR) collects those payments and shares a portion of the revenue with the state where the forest is located. Under federal law, 25% of these receipts are returned to the state, to be used for public schools and public roads in the counties where the land is situated. This structure ensures that the communities who host and support National Forest lands—especially rural counties—receive financial support tied to local resource development. What makes this program unique is that payments occur automatically, without any application process. Payments are calculated from actual mineral leasing receipts and distributed to states and the Forest Service according to long standing statutory formulas. The funding is predictable, formula driven, and directly connected to the mineral activity occurring on National Forest acquired lands,…
items.who: There is no application process. State governments receive these funds automatically when revenue is received from acquired National Forest land leasing.
items.uses: To be used as the state legislature prescribed for the benefit of the public schools and public roads of the country or counties in which such National Forest is situated.

items.title: National Petroleum Reserve - Alaska
items.summary: The Federal Government shares 50 percent of NPR-A oil and gas mineral leasing revenue with the State of Alaska. Royalties are to be paid monthly, and subject to late disbursement interest. Bonuses, rentals, and other non-royalty revenues are paid semi-annually.
items.description: NPR-A is a 23 million acre energy-rich region on Alaska’s North Slope set aside in 1923 and now managed by the Department of the Interior. Under federal law, the Office of Natural Resources Revenue (ONRR) distributes 50 percent of all NPR-A mineral leasing revenues to the State of Alaska, including royalties, bonuses, rentals, and other payments. These funds help Alaska support vital public services and community infrastructure in areas most directly affected by energy development. What makes this program unique is its direct revenue-sharing structure: instead of grants or competitive awards, payments flow from federal energy production straight to the State through a formula established in statute. This ensures predictable, transparent support to communities impacted by NPR-A development, while enabling continued responsible stewardship of federal energy resources.
items.who: Only the State of Alaska is eligible to receive assistance under the National Petroleum Reserve–Alaska (NPR-A) listing.
items.uses: To be used for (1) planning; (2) construction, maintenance, and operation of essential public facilities; and (3) other necessary provisions of public service, giving priority to use by subdivisions of the State most directly or severely impacted by development of oil and gas leasing.

items.title: WaterSMART (Sustain and Manage America’s Resources for Tomorrow)

items.description: The Desert Terminal Lakes Program was established to provide water and related restoration support to at‑risk natural desert terminal lakes in Nevada. The program primarily serves tribal governments, environmental organizations, and regional water‑management partners engaged in restoring and sustaining terminal lake ecosystems. What makes the Desert Terminal Lakes Program unique is its targeted mission: supporting terminal lakes whose closed‑basin nature makes them among the most sensitive and hydrologically constrained waterbodies in the region. The authority for the program has now ended, and all funding has been fully obligated.

items.description: The Colorado River Basin Salinity Control Program is a longstanding partnership led by Reclamation that works to reduce the amount of salt entering the Colorado River system, protecting water quality for millions of municipal, industrial, and agricultural users by improving off-farm systems like canal and ditch lining. What makes the program unique is its basinwide collaboration among federal agencies, states, tribes, and hundreds of local partners, along with its proven success in removing more than 1.3 million tons of salt from the river system each year through practical, science-based solutions.

items.description: The Central Utah Project Completion Act (CUPCA) is contained within Titles II through VI of the Reclamation Projects Authorization and Adjustment Act of 1992 (Public Law 102-575). Its purpose is to provide for the orderly completion of the Central Utah Project (CUP), which is the largest participating project of the 1956 Colorado River Storage Project (CRSP). CUPCA does this by authorizing an increase in the appropriations ceiling for CUP, for which Titles III and IV specifically address fish, wildlife, and outdoor recreation mitigation and enhancement opportunities. items.title: Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation
items.summary: The MSCP’s purposes are: (1) Protect the lower Colorado River environment while ensuring the certainty of existing river water and power operations, (2) Address the needs of threatened and endangered wildlife under the Endangered Species Act, and (3) Reduce the likelihood of listing additional species along the lower Colorado River.
items.description: The Lower Colorado River Multi Species Conservation Program (LCR MSCP) is a long term partnership that balances use of the Colorado River with the conservation of native species and their habitats. Implemented over a 50-year period, the program accommodates current water diversions and power production and will optimize opportunities for future water and power development by providing Endangered Species Act compliance through the implementation of a Habitat Conservation Plan. The program area extends over 400 miles of the lower Colorado River from Lake Mead to the southernmost border with Mexico. The Habitat Conservation Plan calls for the creation of over 8,100 acres of habitat for fish and wildlife species and the production of over 1.2 million native fish to augment existing populations. The plan will benefit at least 27 species, most of which are state or federally listed endangered, threatened, or sensitive species. The Bureau of Reclamation is the implementing agency for the LCR MSCP Steering Committee and permittees which include state and Federal agencies, water and power users, municipalities, Native American tribes, conservation organizations, and other interested…
items.who: State and local governments, nonprofit organizations and institutions, public and private institutions and organizations, Federally recognized Indian Tribal Governments, individuals, small businesses, for-profit organizations, and Native American Organizations.
items.uses: The planning area for the LCR MSCP is defined as areas up to and including the full-pool elevations of Lakes Mead, Mohave, and Havasu and the historical floodplain of the Colorado River from Lake Mead downstream to the Southerly International Boundary with Mexico. The planning area provides habitat for Covered Species listed as endangered or threatened under the ESA; additionally there are region specific species that are inclusive of this program. Visit http://www.lcrmscp.gov for specific information.

items.summary: The objective of this program is to develop and implement management strategies for the Las Vegas Wash to improve water quality, habitat integrity, and reduce the salinity and sediment transport while providing environmental enhancement and recreational opportunities.
items.description: The objective of this program is to develop and implement management strategies for the Las Vegas Wash to improve water quality, habitat integrity, and reduce the salinity and sediment transport while providing environmental enhancement and recreational opportunities. The Las Vegas Wash Coordination Committee has decided that the SNWA will be the lead agency for receiving funding for this program due to the high costs and types of environmental improvement and enhancement, and ability to maintain restoration projects. The Las Vegas Wash Program plays an important role in environmental and water resource issues in Southern Nevada. Historically, the Las Vegas was an ephemeral stream carrying storm flows from the Las Vegas Valley to Lake Mead and the Colorado River. Urban development over the past 60 years has resulted in the formation of the wetlands that helped remove nutrients from these wastewater flows. As the rate of discharges increased, erosion also increased, gradually destroying the existing natural treatment systems and wildlife habitat and creating a large delta in the Las Vegas Bay of Lake Mead. Accelerating erosion, declining water quality, and loss habitat are some of…

items.title: Eastern New Mexico Rural Water System
items.summary: Provide potable surface water to communities in Eastern New Mexico.
items.description: Eastern New Mexico Water Utility Authority was formed for the sole purpose of administration of this new water supply project for the surrounding communities. The Project would pipe 16,450 acre-feet of surface water per year from Ute Reservoir to the eastern New Mexico municipalities of Clovis, Elida, Portales, and Texico currently relying on the declining quantity and quality of the Ogallala Aquifer. Roosevelt County, and Cannon Air Force Base (CAFB) are also beneficiaries of the Project. The present population of the Project service area is about 60,000 people.

items.title: Cooperative Watershed Management
items.popular: Cooperative Watershed Management Program or CWMP
items.summary: Reclamation’s WaterSMART Cooperative Watershed Management program (CWMP) provides funding for the establishment or enlargement of grassroots, local watershed groups to encourage diverse stakeholders to develop collaborative solutions to address their water management needs. A watershed group is a self-sustaining, non-regulatory group that is composed of a diverse array of stakeholders, which may include, but is not…
items.description: Reclamation’s WaterSMART Cooperative Watershed Management program (CWMP) provides funding for the development of grassroots, local watershed groups to encourage diverse stakeholders to develop collaborative solutions to address their water management needs. A watershed group is a self-sustaining, non-regulatory group that is composed of a diverse array of stakeholders, which may include, but is not limited to, private property owners, non-profit organizations, Federal, State, or local agencies, and Tribes. Funding is provided on a competitive basis for the development of new and existing watershed groups, watershed restoration planning, and watershed management project design.
items.who: Existing watershed groups and entities sponsoring the establishment of a watershed group. The watershed group must be located in one of the following states or territories: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wyoming, American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, the Virgin Islands, and Puerto Rico. Existing watershed groups must meet the definition of a watershed group under Section 6002 of the Cooperative Watershed Management Act: the watershed group must be a grassroots, non-regulatory entity that addresses water availability and quality issues…
items.uses: Funding may be used to establish or enlarge a watershed group, perform stakeholder outreach, gather information and collect data regarding watershed conditions, develop bylaws, a mission statement, watershed management project concepts, a watershed restoration plan; and complete watershed management project design work. Funds may also be used to pay the salary of up to 1 full-time employee of the watershed group and any legal fees arising from the establishment of the watershed group as a legal entity.

items.title: Applied Science Grants
items.summary: The objective of the Applied Science Grants is to provide funding to non-Federal entities for the development of tools and information to support water management. Eligible projects include the development of modeling and forecasting tools, hydrologic data platforms, new data sets, and cloud seeding.
items.description: The Applied Science Grants provides funding to non-Federal entities to improve access to and use of hydrologic data, develop and improve water management tools, and improve hydrologic modeling and forecasting capabilities. Water managers and reservoir operators rely on hydrologic data, modeling, and water supply forecasts to make decisions to meet future water demands. Water supply forecasts are estimates of current and future water supplies based on measured basin conditions (e.g., such as the quantity of upstream mountain snowpack). Results from these projects will be used by water managers to increase water supply reliability to meet water delivery requirements (e.g., compacts, decrees, etc.), provide flexibility in water operations to be more resilient during droughts, and enhance water supply forecasts to better predict floods and optimize limited water supplies. Example projects include improving operational models for irrigation water deliveries or reservoir operations, improving the use of snow monitoring technologies to enhance the skill of water supply forecasts, and improving data acquisition, data analysis, and data delivery, including the development of hydrologic…
items.who: See above.
items.uses: Through Applied Science Grants, Reclamation provides cost-shared financial assistance on a competitive basis for projects to develop tools and information for: (1) assessing water availability and quality, (2) assessing risks to water supplies from drought and other water management challenges (e.g., invasive species, sedimentation, managing to meet competing water demands, meeting endangered species requirements, etc.), and (3) assessing and evaluating watershed management practices.

items.title: New Mexico Rio Grande Basin Pueblos Irrigation Infrastructure
items.summary: Rehabilitate and repair irrigation infrastructure of the Rio Grande Pueblos to conserve water and help address potential conflicts over water in the Rio Grande Basin.
items.description: Under the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009, Congress authorized $4 million to conduct a study of the irrigation infrastructure within the 18 Rio Grande pueblos, and $6 million in each of ten subsequent years to address identified infrastructure improvements. The Act required a study report to be submitted to Congress including a list of projects recommended for implementation. Initially, detailed physical surveys of the existing irrigation infrastructure at each pueblo were completed. Most of the surveys have now been completed but remaining areas will be surveyed as specific project need arises. The study report identified nearly $280 million in irrigation improvements, at a 2017 pricing level, needed on pueblo lands. These improvements are important to the Tribal economies, to preserving their cultural traditions for future generations, and to maximize water conservation in the Rio Grande Basin. The report was finalized in June 2022 and submitted to Congress by the Department of the Interior's Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs. Since that time, the program has received consistent funding and projects continue to be implemented on tribal lands throughout the Rio…

items.title: Suisun Marsh Preservation Agreement
items.summary: Execute and implement the agreement between the Department of the Interior, the State of California, and the Suisun Resource Conservation District to ensure a dependable water supply of adequate quantity and quality for the protection and preservation of Suisan Marsh fish and wildlife habitat in accordance with PL 99-546, State and Water Resources Control Board Decision 1641, and the Revised Suisun Marsh…
items.description: The purpose of this agreement is to carry out Public Law 99-546 and the Suisun Marsh Preservation Agreement with California Department of Water Resources, California Department of Fish and Wildlife, and the Suisun Resource Conservation District. Suisun Marsh is the largest contiguous brackish water marsh in the western United States, covering about 116,000 acres. The ecosystem there is dependent on a balance of saltwater from the San Francisco Bay and freshwater from the Sacramento River and the San Joaquin River. It is a mix of private and public lands that support recreational activities and agriculture for the regional community.

It was developed through multi-party negotiations in the late 1980s and early 2000s, involving the Taos Pueblo, the State of New Mexico, the Taos Valley Acequia Association (and its 55 member acequias), the Town of Taos, El Prado Water and Sanitation District (EPWSD), the 12 Taos-area Mutual Domestic Water Consumer Associations, and the United States of America in its trust capacity.

items.title: Colorado River System Conservation Pilot
items.summary: This program supports conservation projects that create “system water” through voluntary compensated reductions in water use or provides environmental benefits or restoration of ecosystems or habitats in the Colorado River Basin. Includes Drought Contingency Planning activities to enhance conservation through expanded measurement and monitoring.
items.description: The program is designed to improve water reliability, strengthen water supplies, and foster resilience to drought conditions within the Colorado River Basin. Funding comes from two major federal laws—the Inflation Reduction Act and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act—which support modernizing water infrastructure, expanding and enhancing water supplies, and restoring ecosystems or habitats. Targeted support backs projects that address challenges from strained water sources by strengthening conservation practices and enhancing sustainability. Investments in planning, design, and construction enable communities to use water more efficiently and ensure reliable supplies over time, helping to reduce pressure on existing systems, improve drought preparedness, and promote responsible stewardship of water resources. Assistance Listing 15.567 is available to state, Tribal, regional, and local public entities that manage water resources. This program stands out by combining two historic federal investments, accelerating projects that bring both immediate and long-term benefits to areas facing drought.
items.who: Eligibility of the Upper Colorado River Commission established through PL 117-328.
items.uses: Pursuant to PL117-328 – Pilot projects are authorized to be funded through grants to public entities that use water from the Colorado River Basin for municipal purposes for projects that are implemented by 1 or more non-Federal entities or grants or other appropriate financial agreements to provide additional funds for renewing or implementing water conservation agreements that are in existence on the date of enactment of this Act.

items.summary: The CALFED Water Use Efficiency Grant program promotes projects that emphasize water use efficiency and conservation activities that result in benefits for the California-Bay Delta.
items.description: Serving Water Districts, Cities, or any entity with water delivery authority. Continuous improvement, maintenance, and operational support to improve the use of water resources. Develop and support methods to use water more efficiently and support the update of water delivery facilities to the latest technology. Focusing on increasing water supply through efficiency at every level. Proposals may include any type of implementation, demonstration, pilot water use efficiency, or conservation projects that have benefits to the California Bay-Delta. Projects that only consist of research or feasibility studies, planning or education will not be funded. Financial assistance is limited to $500,000 or less, per year. For further information, please contact the regional office.
items.who: Applicants must be located in the CALFED solution area. For the geographic extent of the CALFED Solution Area please refer to the map available at https://www.usbr.gov/mp/watershare/docs/calfed-solution-area.pdf.

items.title: Salton Sea Program
items.summary: Objectives of this program are to develop and implement restoration and management strategies at the Salton Sea that (1) enhance fish and wildlife health, (2) protect air quality, (3) provide opportunities for recreation use and economic development, and (4) maintain a secure Colorado River water supply.
items.description: The Salton Sea Program provides funding to U.S. States, Tribes, nonprofit organizations, and research institutions to develop and implement dust suppression, habitat restoration, and management strategies at the Salton Sea to safeguard public health and improve air quality for neighboring communities, as well as to support long-term habitat restoration efforts for fish and wildlife.

items.title: Agricultural Water Use Efficiency Program
items.summary: The objective of the Agricultural Water Conservation Efficiency Program is to invite eligible applicants to leverage their money and resources by cost sharing with Reclamation on projects that save water, improve water management, increase water supply reliability, improve energy efficiency, and benefit endangered species. Projects that achieve this by directly enabling on-farm water conservation or water use…
items.description: Invite Indian tribes, irrigation districts, water districts, and other organizations with water or power delivery authority to leverage their money and resources by cost sharing with Reclamation on projects that seek to: • Conserve and use agricultural water more efficiently, • Mitigate conflict risk in areas at a high risk of future water conflict, • Enable farmers to make on-farm improvements that may be eligible for USDA’s Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) funding, and • Contribute benefits to water supply reliability in the Western United States. Project sponsors leverage their money and resources by cost-sharing with Reclamation to construct on-farm projects that save water, improve water management, increase water supply reliability, improve energy efficiency, and benefit endangered species. Funded projects result in quantifiable and sustained agricultural water savings and support broader water reliability benefits. The AWUE program supports Reclamation’s priorities, including: • Increasing agricultural water supplies, • Leveraging science and technology to improve water supply reliability for farmers, and • Addressing drought impacts on agricultural activities.
